newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kisangani -- strategic prize in Zaire's war.
newsitem.headline: Kisangani -- strategic prize in Zaire's war.

text.p: Zaire's third city of Kisangani, its jungle setting immortalised in Joseph Conrad's bleak novel "Heart of Darkness", is a strategic prize targeted by rebels vowing to topple veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko.

The nerve centre of army operations in the war zone, it is perched strategically at the head a major navigable stretch of the mighty Zaire River that flows west from there to the capital Kinshasa -- some 1,500 km (900 miles) downstream.
A lack of passable roads through the sprawling Central African nation's jungle and bush makes the Zaire River and its many tributaries the principal arteries for internal and external trade.
These are its main historical and geographical features.

-- Kisangani was formerly known as Stanleyville after the 19th century explorer Henry Morton Stanley, who won fame tracing missing missionary David Livingstone in the African jungle and spearheaded European colonisation of what is modern-day Zaire.

-- Officials put its population at 500,000, making the city Zaire's third largest after the capital Kinshasa and the southern Shaba mining capital of Lumumbashi. Some say Mbuji Mayi, capital of diamond rich Kasai, rivals it for third place.

-- The capital of Upper Zaire, Kisangani is the nation's second most important port after Matadi on the Atlantic Ocean; the main inland port, it is a gateway to the interior -- a forest and farming region, trading in timber, gold and gems.

-- Kisangani boasts one of Zaire's four international airports but years of central government neglect and economic decay have reduced it to a shell of its former self, resembling more a series of forest villages than a major urban centre.

-- Kisangani's jungle surroundings were immortalised in Conrad's famous novel "Heart of Darkness", which describes a river journey into the thick equatorial rain forest when Belgian King Leopold held sway over the country as his personal domain.

-- Kisangani lived up to its "heart of darkness" reputation after independence in 1960 when it bore the brunt of a series of rebellions; much blood was spilled in the city both during the revolts and when Belgian paratroopers and mercenaries brought the city to heel in 1965, months before Mobutu seized power.

-- During that period, the city was capital of a breakaway republic led by allies of assassinated independence leader Patrice Lumumba. At one stage the Lumumbists controlled as much as two-thirds of the country.
-- Army-led looting in the city in 1991 and 1993 crippled many local businesses and sent much of the region's expatriate business community away.
-- A fresh round of looting by soldiers fleeing rebels in the east last November further crippled the local economy.
